items.title: Abolish Lock Poisoning
items.content_html:
Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex, the mutex is poisoned. That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError. The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state.

Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.

In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.

Primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning.

Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.”

When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all.

That’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only issue with the system today. So here I want to share some of the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten.

The Error Holds the Lock

One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock!

That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box<dyn Error> or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives (#159930).

This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server.

Panic To Outage

Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless:

  • In RLS a failed cargo build panicked with ENV_LOCK held which made any subsequent runs impossible.
  • Mozilla’s application-services saw PoisonError rise to rank 5 in crash stats and moved to parking_lot after they concluded they did not benefit of poisoning handling.
  • A Neon safekeeper on staging failed every timeline lookup after a panic with a global lock held, and the original panic could not even be found in the logs.

While not live services, test suites show the same general issue. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError. This problem showed up for cargo, deno, polars and rustc itself.

Attempt At Recovery

If you recover with into_inner(), the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

Nobody Relies on It, Not Even std

So who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015, two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Same with the panic output capture, the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock. They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison.

And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison. When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing.” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

Wasmtime, crossbeam-channel, tracing-subscriber always ignores lock poisoning. rust-analyzer switched to parking_lot after cancellation poisoned its solver like RLS did before. The parking_lot maintainer described it as an anti-feature that hurts usability and reliability to which I strongly concur.

Why Only Mutex?

Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell. Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

Take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell, and you have exactly the same problem. Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError, the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the issue.

Given how much panic catching goes on in async code, much of which is !Send for performance reasons, I’m not even convinced that panics get caught more often in multi-threaded code yet nobody asks for RefCell to poison.

The standard library isn’t consistent with itself either as LazyLock poisons for good, OnceLock never poisons, Mutex poisons but lets you recover.

Also remember that poisoning only tracks panics and a more common early return has the same issue. The ? operator (as well as the try! macro before) that returns early from the middle of a critical section leaves the same broken invariant behind an unpoisoned lock.

Note also that the coupling of poisoning of mutexes is historical and an explicit Poison<T> type would allow you to opt into this for any interior mutability wrapper.

What I want

Personally I hope the rust team stabilizes std::sync::nonpoison, have std::sync::Mutex resolve to it by default. If someone wants poisoning add that separate Poison<T> wrapper then anyone who believes they need and can handle it, can opt into it for any type including RefCell or tokio threads.

What I think would be the worst of all outcomes is the counter-proposal is to keep poisoning but have lock() panic instead of returning a Result. That would only fix the held guard lock semantics, and to a smaller degree the ergonomics, but it makes the slow outage the only option. That is what every lock().unwrap() does today, and the issues above should be plenty of evidence of this being a problematic behavior in light of the existence of catch_unwind.

The post In defense of lock poisoning is the best argument for the other side and worth reading but I believe the evidence all points the other way, and most of what Oxide ships aborts on panic anyway which is also a reasonable behavior.

items.title: The pleasure of knowing
items.summary:
There is an inherent pleasure in knowing things.

It might be more expedient to externalize your understanding to others: to other people, or to machines. It might be more productive. In many cases, it will be more realistic to not understand things, but to delegate to others to understand for you. And some things you will not want to understand, or you may want to understand but not want to pay the full cost of understanding (for example, a topic which would require you to invest a lot of study time, but where your actual level of interest isn’t that big).

But: in many cases, this abandonment of understanding will lead to less pleasure. It will be like having injected a required number of calories for survival vs. having had an ice cream. Both satisfy a need, but humans prefer to have ice cream.

We are in a period of human history where you can be paid to understand things, in some professions even without much ritual or formality. Particularly deep understanding commands a decent salary and respect within your industry.

The times are changing. In some places, it is more economical to pay a machine to provide sufficient output. You might say: well that’s not a problem, there’s no shortage of interesting questions to ask, you can just try to understand other things and get paid for that, but actually no, you cannot. You don’t get to pick the topics that interest you, the same way you don’t pick which food you crave or which person you fall in love with. And moreover, only a small portion of the economy is about being paid to understand, and even within those fields which are almost explicitly about that, there’s a lot that happens that isn’t about you understanding, but is more about producing some output and having partial overlap with a quest to understand.

All that is beside the point. The economy is one thing. Individual experience is another thing. The fact that certain professions have existed and proliferated based on the fact that people in these professions know things – that’s a historical oddity, especially if you take in consideration the proportion of such professionals in the overall working force. It’s a blip in human history that “engineers” exist, and learning and knowing things have been private obsessions without any economic guarantee extended to such individuals, for a long, long time.

I reiterate: there’s a pleasure in learning, and understanding things. When you look at something, and you ask yourself “I wonder how this works”, there’s a sense of unsated curiosity, a sense of directedness at the question, a subjective feeling of annoyance for not knowing. Whatever the economics of having a human understand something vs. giving it to someone in another country to understand vs. giving it to a country that exists only in a data center to understand – the human, some human will always crave this understanding, the same way most humans will crave the ice cream, however more expedient it be for them to simply hook up to an IV that provides all their caloric needs.

This human will look at a question and the question will nag them, the question will bother them, the question will exist in their mind and want to resolve itself. That other people or machines understand the answer to that question plays no role in the life of this person. The fact that someone somewhere understands exactly how and why gravity works does not reduce the curiosity that I posses about gravity. The fact that this is a someone smart also doesn’t change it. The fact that a von Neumann understood physics and mathematics to a degree that I probably never will does not abate my curiosity, and does not sate it. The hunger for knowledge is still there, the thirst for understanding is still there. The fact that a Claude Opus 5.5 knows something or that a Jupiter-brained, Dyson-sphere-wielding machine superintelligence knows something – none of these things play any role in my life, except maybe in me having a vague sense that, if you really need some work output to happen that’s based on that understanding, you have other options besides me. You have other people, or other machines that you could ask, that might give you a better answer. The thirst and consequent pleasure of understanding is about me, it’s about my experience and my desire. It’s not sated the same way that I don’t stop craving ice cream when you tell me that an Olympic athlete, whom I will never best in a physical competition, had ice cream. I didn’t have it, and I still want it.

I feel like I am standing before a looming, future, giant, omniscient deity and my puny little intellectual curiosity is merely the hunger of a small field mouse, trumped by the hunger of a massive combine harvester before it. And yet, when the harvester finishes a field, I myself am no less hungry, and I still climb the flowers and lick the nectar, and eat the berries and seeds, and still I crave the pleasure of knowing.

items.title: AI and Irontown
items.content_html:
For our last movie night we watched Princess Mononoke. I remembered loving that movie when I was younger, but watching it as an adult made me once again realize how Miyazaki has a way of expressing diverging sides without picking one. The film shows people, animals and spirits with legitimate and largely incompatible needs, and each faction is further engaged in infighting.

A central arc of the story is Lady Eboshi’s Irontown, which gives people who were largely rejected by society work, protection and dignity. She gives shelter and work to those who have leprosy and to former sex workers. The mine and the weapon factory provide them with a livelihood, but they also destroy the forest around them. The forest’s inhabitants, in particular the boars, response choose war against the humans to defend themselves. Eboshi is not portrayed as a villain. She does real good for the people of Irontown, but also is an arms manufacturer who is destroying the forest around it.

The film anchors around a character called Ashitaka, who has been condemned to death by an unfortunate encounter with a god that was turned into a demon after being fatally wounded by one of Eboshi’s guns. He doesn’t take sides, but he wants to understand and find the truth. Another character is San (whom they call Mononoke), a girl who was raised by wolves and, despite being human, considers herself part of the forest.

This movie’s backdrop is human progress, and it reminded me so much of the challenges we are facing today with AI. AI is useful, empowering and consequential beyond the people who benefit from it. It’s similar to the iron in the story. Irontown gives the outcast purpose and power. There are people today who see themselves in an environment just like that: people who were never let in before and who can now build things that were out of reach. They are wielding AI to their benefit. But there are negative externalities. In Mononoke it’s not just the spirits and animals in the forest who bear the consequences, it’s also other people. Irontown produces guns, and its people are engaged in fights with other humans. There is conflict and power seeking everywhere.

Another, unseen character is the power-hungry emperor, who wants the head of the forest spirit, a god, because he believes it will make him immortal. Eboshi is willing to support that cause, not because she thinks it’s right, but because she is at war with the forest’s gods who are preventing her expansion, so they have a common interest. But there really is no need for anyone to kill the forest spirit, in the same way there is no need for any one country to “win at AI”. What drives it is the fear of what happens if someone else wins first. And the emperor is willing to have a god killed for it. The people who help him with that desire, Eboshi included, don’t understand the chaos it will unleash.

There it also shows the dangers of seeking overwhelming power without comprehension of how to control its consequences. The pursuit of power itself becomes destructive. In the end, the gods die, and what grows back is not the old forest anymore. Irontown is destroyed. Eboshi wants to rebuild it, and to build a better town this time. Ashitaka stays with the people of Irontown after his curse is lifted by the dying forest spirit. San cannot forgive the humans and stays with the wolves. In the end, nothing is truly resolved, but there is a truce that came at great cost.

Ashitaka’s role in the movie is one of a neutral actor. He was wronged both by a spirit turned demon in the forest, who put a curse on him, and, indirectly, by Eboshi, who caused the spirit to turn evil. Yet he harbors no ill will towards either side. He sets out to “see with eyes unclouded by hate,” and in the course of the movie he is seen as an unaligned actor. He helps people on both sides, and stands in their way to prevent further conflict. He doesn’t feel like a pacifist, but he’s the closest to one there is. He’s a truth seeker in a changing world. Because he engages he’s seen as suspicious by both sides, and ends up shot by the people of Irontown when he tries to rescue San.

I use AI every day and find it genuinely empowering. But I also recognize the pain it causes some, and the moral problems it poses. It’s genuine progress for humanity, but it comes at significant cost. And many of those costs will be carried by people who aren’t going to benefit from it.

So it’s no surprise that AI feels like a threat to many today. Communities currently strongly align themselves with one side and fight against the other. The forest spirit did not have to die and the boars did not have to die in a senseless war.

The question is not whether there will be iron, but what kind of Irontown we build with it. I want our conversation about AI to make room for nuance and genuine understanding, for us to look at it and each other with eyes unclouded by hate. We should take advantage of its real benefits, but also recognize the damage it can do, and the choices we still have about what we build and what we’re willing to sacrifice for it. I like to think there is a path for people with differing opinions can find a way to live alongside before losing something we can’t get back.
